 AMD CEO Lisa Su says, 'We are a data center-first company'
 With record Data Center revenue it makes sense that AMD CEO Lisa Su would say 'We are a data center-first company,' but it's still disappointing to hear.
 VIEW GALLERY - 2 AMD CEO Lisa Su stands before an EPYC processor graphic, underscoring the data center focus she described after AMD reported record Data Center revenue. Kosta Andreadis Senior Editor Published Nov 10, 2026 12:56 AM CST 1-minute read time What you need to know
 AMD's record $8.5 billion in Data Center revenue and weaker gaming and consumer prospects underpin Lisa Su's description of the company as data center-first. She says AMD aims to double its data center business by 2027 while continuing consumer and gaming products despite the downturn.

"We are a data center-first company, that is our profile, and people need more computing to power all these applications," AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a recent interview with Yahoo Finance . The interview followed the company's latest financial report and earnings call, where the company's record $8.5 billion in Data Center revenue delivered record growth for Q3 2026.

 2 AMD CEO Lisa Su holds up a processor onstage; she recently described AMD as a “data center-first company” following record Data Center revenue. VIEW GALLERY - 2 IMAGES With Gaming revenue down 40% and the current memory and component crisis set to deliver a double-digit decline for AMD's client and consumer business (which includes Ryzen and Radeon), that statement makes sense through a financial lens. Especially when Lisa Su adds that AMD is looking to double its data center-related business as we head into 2027. And it all comes down to compute.
 Read more : AMD posts record revenue in Q3 2025: client and gaming segment is up 73% since last year 
 Read more : AMD's gaming revenue drops 40%, says PC market will decline by double-digit percentage in 2027 
 Read more : AMD's Client and Gaming segment had a record 2025, driven by demand for Ryzen processors 
 "What I look at is in the long term, if you believe - which I do, deeply - that computing in many ways equates to intelligence," Lisa Su adds. "The more compute you have, the more intelligent you are, the more intelligent your company is, the more problems you're going to be able to solve, the more you're going to accelerate your business." Now, this doesn't mean that AMD is going to exit the consumer or gaming markets, as AMD has quite a bit on the horizon - next-gen Zen 6-powered processors for desktop and mobile, RDNA 5 graphics cards for gaming and AI, and custom hardware for Sony's PlayStation 6 and Microsoft's Xbox Project Helix.

 Which parts of AMD's data center business are driving its growth?
 Demand for compute, particularly AI and data center infrastructure, is driving AMD's growth. Its Data Center business delivered a record $8.5 billion in revenue in Q3 2026, though the story does not break that growth down by product or service. With shortages and prices for things like memory and storage rising sharply, the consumer PC market is in widespread decline. Even with the downturn, AMD is better positioned than most, thanks to strong demand for Ryzen. And even though AI and data centers are driving unprecedented growth, AMD seems all in, with Lisa Su's comments focused on the long-term vision of AI and compute infrastructure becoming "essential to every aspect of our lives and every aspect of our business."
